column1: In a G7→Cmaj7 resolution, what exact half-step motions do the guide tones make?
column2: B (3rd of G7) rises a half step to C (root of Cmaj7); F (7th of G7) falls a half step to E (3rd of Cmaj7) — contrary motion by the smallest possible interval.

column1: Why do jazz pianists voice chords around the 3rd and 7th instead of root and 5th?
column2: The 3rd and 7th ('guide tones') carry the chord's quality (major/minor/dominant) and the tension-resolution motion; the root and 5th are harmonically redundant structural tones, especially since the bassist already states the root.

column1: What is the three-note 'shell' voicing for a seventh chord, and which tone is omitted?
column2: Root, 3rd, and 7th — the 5th is omitted because it adds almost no harmonic information and clutters the hand.

column1: Why is the tritone (3rd to 7th of a dominant chord) acoustically unstable?
column2: It spans exactly 600 cents — the exact midpoint of the octave in 12-tone equal temperament — with no simple small-number ratio to anchor it, so the ear cannot settle it into a stable interval and hears it as needing resolution.

column1: What is the acoustic/physics explanation for why parallel fifths and octaves are avoided in voice leading?
column2: When two voices move in lockstep a fifth or octave apart, they fuse perceptually into a single sound, causing the ear to lose track of one independent melodic strand.

column1: What is tritone substitution, and why does it work?
column2: Replacing a dominant chord with another dominant chord a tritone away (e.g., G7 → Db7) because both chords share the identical 3rd/7th tritone (B–F in G7 is enharmonically F–Cb in Db7); the ear tracks the tritone's collapse, not the root motion.

column1: Why can diminished 7th chords and augmented triads function as 'wormholes' between keys?
column2: They divide the octave into equal slices (diminished: four equal minor 3rds; augmented: three equal major 3rds), so the identical interval pattern lets the same shape be respelled to resolve toward multiple different keys.

column1: In rootless left-hand voicings, what is the structural difference between 'A form' and 'B form' for a ii–V–I?
column2: A form places the 7th on the bottom of the voicing (e.g., Dm7: F-A-C-E); B form places the 3rd on the bottom, used to avoid awkward hand position or to alternate register (e.g., G7: B-E-F-A).

column1: What makes a pitch an 'avoid note' over a given chord, using F over Cmaj7 as the example?
column2: F creates a minor 9th (half-step-plus-octave) clash against the chord tone E (the 3rd), producing high tension that needs quick resolution if used — the same note (F) is a sweet available tension (the b7) over G7 and a chord tone over Fmaj7.

column1: What is the correct wrist and forearm technique for jazz piano comping, and why does it matter?
column2: Wrist level with the key bed (not drooped or cocked), using forearm-weight drop into the keys rather than isolated finger-pushing; finger-only technique under tempo pressure is the primary cause of carpal tunnel and tendinitis in jazz pianists.

column1: List the voice-leading invariants in priority order for a ii–V–I progression.
column2: 1) Guide tones (3rd & 7th) move by step or hold as common tones. 2) Tritones resolve inward by semitone. 3) Common tones stay in the same voice/register. 4) Prefer contrary motion between outer voices when movement is needed. 5) Roots and 5ths are omitted from comping voicings or left to the bass.

column1: Why does the b7 of a dominant chord (e.g., F in G7) sound unstable and want to resolve, acoustically speaking?
column2: It sits close to the 7th partial of the overtone series built on the root, which is slightly flat and unstable relative to equal temperament, so the ear hears it as 'leaning' toward resolution rather than sitting still.
